title: Atomic & nuclear physics
subtitle: A bounded introductory problem-solving path
prerequisites: Mathematical toolkit, Electricity & magnetism, Quantum II, Relativity. Local mathematical bridges are taught before use; advanced topics retain their stated prerequisites.

lessons.title: Count charge and isotopes
lessons.idea: Changing electrons makes an ion; changing neutrons makes another isotope.
body: Think of the nucleus as an identity label: its proton count chooses the element. Electrons surround it; removing one changes charge, not the element.
An isotope keeps the same proton count but has a different neutron count. Mass number counts nucleons, not electrons, and is not the measured mass in kilograms.

lessons.title: Translate an energy scale
lessons.idea: A photon connects an energy gap to a frequency and wavelength.
body: An electronvolt is an energy unit, not a voltage. One electron crossing a one-volt potential difference changes its electric potential energy by one electronvolt in magnitude.
A photon with twice the energy has twice the frequency and half the vacuum wavelength. Use consistent units rather than mixing nanometres directly with metres.
lessons.terms: E: photon energy (eV). Electronvolt; 1 eV = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ joule. h: Planck constant (eV s). Use h≈4.136×10⁻¹⁵ eV s. f, c, λ: frequency, vacuum light speed, vacuum wavelength (Hz, m/s, m). Hz means repeats per second; hc≈1240 eV nm; nm is 10⁻⁹ metre.

lessons.title: Read a spectral gap
lessons.idea: A spectral line measures a difference between levels, not either absolute level.
body: Imagine two shelves. The photon tells you the height difference, not the height of the floor. Similarly, adding the same energy offset to every atomic level leaves all transition energies unchanged.
Emission lowers the atom energy and creates a photon. Absorption raises the atom energy when the incoming photon matches an allowed transition within its line width.

lessons.title: Binding needs a reference
lessons.idea: Negative bound-state energy means energy must be supplied to separate the system.
body: Set zero energy at an electron and nucleus very far apart and at rest. A bound state lies below that reference. Its negative energy is not negative mass or an impossible measurement.
Coulomb attraction supplies the potential, but quantum motion supplies kinetic energy. A classical point electron orbiting forever is not the quantum ground-state model.
lessons.terms: U, E, K: potential, total, kinetic energy (J). J means joule; zero potential is at infinite separation. r, Z, e, k: separation, proton count, charge unit, Coulomb constant (m, count, C, N m²/C²). r must be positive; k≈8.99×10⁹ N m²/C².

lessons.title: Label hydrogen states
lessons.idea: Quantum numbers label allowed states rather than tiny planetary paths.
body: For a hydrogen-like atom, choose a principal number n starting at one. The orbital label l can run from zero to n−1. The projection label m runs in integer steps from −l to +l.
These labels describe a wavefunction and angular measurements. A spin label adds two electron spin projections; it does not mean an electron literally spins like a ball.

symbols.description: The dots mean the intervening integer values, not every real number.

apply.title: Explain your decision
apply.text: Does specifying n alone choose one unique state?
apply.answer: Usually not. Different angular and spin labels can share the same principal number and, in the simplest Coulomb model, the same energy.

lessons.title: A shell is not an orbit
lessons.idea: Radial probability includes the amount of space in a spherical shell.
body: Probability density tells how likely a tiny volume is. A shell farther from the centre contains more volume, so its probability also includes a geometrical factor.
For the hydrogen ground state, density is largest at the nucleus, but radial probability is zero at radius zero and peaks away from it. Neither statement draws an electron trajectory.
lessons.terms: P(r)dr: probability in a thin spherical shell (no unit). dr is a small positive thickness in metres. r, ψ, π: radius, ground-state wavefunction, circle constant (m, m⁻³ᐟ², no unit). The squared magnitude of ψ is density in m⁻³; π≈3.14159.

apply.text: Why can the most likely radius differ from the largest density location?

lessons.idea: A hydrogen transition uses the difference of inverse-square level energies.
body: In the nonrelativistic one-electron model, higher n levels lie closer to zero. The gaps shrink as n increases; equally spaced labels do not imply equally spaced energies.
The approximate 13.6 eV constant is for hydrogen. A nucleus with charge Z gives a Z² factor in the infinite-nuclear-mass model; reduced-mass corrections matter for precision.
lessons.terms: En: energy of level n relative to ionization (eV). Negative values are bound. Z, n: nuclear proton count and principal number (counts). This formula assumes only one electron.

lessons.title: Allowed does not mean certain
lessons.idea: A selection rule can make one coupling vanish without predicting a guaranteed transition.
body: Light couples states through an interaction. If the relevant matrix element is zero by symmetry, that mechanism cannot produce the transition in the ideal model.

For electric-dipole hydrogen transitions, orbital l changes by one. A transition satisfying that rule still needs a nonzero strength, an available photon energy and the right population; other mechanisms have other rules.

lessons.title: Two kinds of angular momentum
lessons.idea: Orbital angular momentum and intrinsic spin are different quantum observables.
body: Orbital angular momentum describes the spatial wavefunction under rotation. Electron spin is an intrinsic two-state property; it is not a path around the nucleus.
A chosen-axis measurement gives a projection, not the full vector magnitude. For l=1 the magnitude is √2 times ħ, while the largest axis projection is only ħ.
lessons.terms: L, Lz: orbital magnitude and chosen-axis projection (J s). Angular momentum units are joule seconds. l, m, ħ: orbital number, projection number, reduced Planck constant (no unit, no unit, J s). ħ=h/(2π); √ means positive square root.

lessons.title: Couple spin to orbital motion
lessons.idea: Spin-orbit energy depends on the way two angular momenta combine.
body: An effective spin-orbit interaction links the electron intrinsic spin to its orbital motion. We label their total by j rather than assigning two little mechanical arrows.
For an electron with l=1 and spin s=1/2, the total j can be 1/2 or 3/2. Their different coupling energies can split a previously single level.

lessons.title: Split levels with a field
lessons.idea: A weak magnetic field can give different energies to different magnetic projections.
body: A magnetic moment interacts with an external field. In a weak-field atomic model, each magnetic sublevel shifts in proportion to its projection label.
The sign and size use a specified factor g. This is a weak-field description: sufficiently strong fields can change which angular labels are useful.

lessons.title: Resolve smaller structure
lessons.idea: Fine and hyperfine structure refer to different physical corrections.

Fine structure includes relativistic and electron spin-orbit corrections. Hyperfine structure involves nuclear moments interacting with electronic degrees of freedom. Neither word simply means a narrower instrument setting.

lessons.title: Fill states not locations
lessons.idea: Pauli exclusion restricts occupation of complete one-electron states.
body: Identical electrons are not individually tagged. In an independent-electron picture, each complete spatial-and-spin state can hold at most one electron.
One spatial orbital offers two different spin states, so it can hold two electrons with opposite spin labels. The rule is not that two electrons can never be found in the same region of space.

lessons.title: Screen the nuclear pull
lessons.idea: Other electrons modify the attraction an electron experiences.
body: A nucleus attracts an electron, while other electrons repel it. A simple average model replaces this complicated environment with an effective nuclear charge.
That effective charge is not a changed proton count. Different orbitals penetrate the inner electron cloud differently, so one universal value cannot describe every state accurately.

lessons.title: Use filling to explain trends
lessons.idea: Electron configurations help explain trends but do not make every trend monotonic.
body: A configuration records occupied orbital families. Outer electrons largely shape chemical behavior because removing or sharing them usually costs less energy than disturbing tightly bound inner electrons.
Across a row, nuclear attraction and screening change together. Shell closures and orbital details create exceptions, so a trend is a reasoned pattern rather than an unbreakable counting rule.

Across a period, increasing effective nuclear attraction usually pulls the outer cloud inward and raises the energy needed to remove an electron. Down a group, an added outer shell usually increases atomic size. Pairing and shell details cause exceptions to simple ionization-energy trends.

Exchange follows from fermion symmetry, while correlation describes additional dependence beyond a chosen independent-particle reference. Improving either is not the same as inventing a new force.

lessons.idea: The same resonant field can stimulate absorption or emission.

A minimum in a potential curve gives a stable equilibrium separation. Small displacements produce a restoring tendency; the molecule still has quantum motion near the minimum.

lessons.title: Nuclear attraction is short ranged
lessons.idea: Nucleons interact strongly at close range, while electric repulsion reaches much farther.
body: Two protons repel electrically. Nuclear binding requires an attractive residual strong interaction over very short distances, with more complicated spin and distance dependence than a simple universal pull.
A nucleon mainly interacts strongly with nearby neighbors. This helps explain approximate saturation: binding does not grow like every nucleon attracting every other equally.

Neutron-proton imbalance and pairing add further terms. This smooth model explains broad trends but misses important shell effects.

Two models can predict similar energies yet disagree on spin or parity. Measuring more than one observable makes the comparison stronger.

The decay probability is conditional on still being present. A nucleus does not become more overdue merely because it has survived a long time in this model.

lessons.idea: Half-life and mean lifetime are different summaries of one exponential law.
body: Half-life is the time at which survival probability becomes one half. Mean lifetime is the average waiting time over many decays.
Because the exponential tail extends to long times, the mean is larger than the median half-life. Neither is a deadline for the last survivor.

In a simplified tunnelling picture, the alpha-like configuration has some chance to pass through a barrier. Positive energy release alone does not determine the escape probability or lifetime.

body: A gamma transition changes an excited nuclear state without changing proton or neutron counts. The photon energy is close to the level gap, but a free nucleus must recoil.
For a heavy nucleus and a small gap relative to its rest energy, recoil energy is tiny but positive. The photon therefore carries slightly less energy than the initial excitation gap.

This uses small relative errors, approximately Gaussian rate uncertainties, independent rates and negligible timing uncertainty; it is not an exact low-count interval.

apply.answer: Additional data can test the exponential shape and expose inconsistent residuals. Two exact points can always fit one amplitude and one decay constant.

lessons.title: Balance and test a synthetic reaction
lessons.idea: A complete reaction check separates count balance, energetics and probability.
body: Use one synthetic example to keep the three questions separate. First identify the residual nucleus from conserved counts, then compare supplied masses, then state what remains unknown.
Do not silently treat a mathematically balanced invented channel as an observed physical reaction. This exercise tests reasoning, not isotope data recall.

check.prompt: What does the positive Q establish here?
options: Rest-energy release is available if the specified channel occurs
explanations: Correct. Positive Q establishes available rest-energy release for that specified channel.
Kinematic energy release does not establish a reaction rate or certainty.
Detector efficiency is a separate measurement parameter.

apply.answer: Beam conditions, target population, cross section, geometry, detector efficiency and backgrounds are needed; count and energy balance alone do not provide a rate.

lessons.title: Compare the models
lessons.idea: Choose a model by scale, observable and assumptions rather than by its impressive name.
body: Atomic lines mainly involve electronic energy structure, while nuclear lines and decays involve nuclear states and interactions. Both require quantum reasoning, but their characteristic scales and useful approximations differ.
A good answer names what is being predicted and what is omitted. More complicated is not automatically better if its parameters are unknown or its regime is wrong.

check.prompt: Which is the best first response to a mismatch with data?
options: Assume every measured point is wrong
Check assumptions, inputs and uncertainties before declaring new physics
Add more digits to the same answer
explanations: Measurements deserve uncertainty checks, not automatic dismissal.
Correct. A mismatch can arise from invalid assumptions, input errors or uncertainty before requiring new physics.
More digits do not repair an inappropriate or inaccurate model.

apply.title: Explain your decision
apply.text: How would you explain a bounded model to another learner?
apply.answer: Say what it predicts, its inputs, its physical regime and one failure case. Then compare a changed example rather than only repeating its name.
